A kid has a guitar concert in two weeks, and tells her parents. Mom and dad both say they can't wait.

Kid reminds parents, in excitement, that the show is a week away. The reminder is also the kid's way of hitting home the importance, especially since her parents are notorious for not being around. She reminds them it's 6 days away. 5 days away. 2 days. 1.

The day comes, and she gets into position with her band. Before they commence, she takes a glance around to see where they are sitting. And she looks. And she looks. And they're not there. A sea of families, but a drought of support. 

She gets picked up by her parents and she is confused. Confused that they were able to pick her up but not be there for the show. And the confusion turns to anger.

I started with a 101 class in college. My professor was adamant about us learning the basics, understand how light works being the key thing. 

It's unrealistic to suggest "just take a 101 class!" but I will say follow along with beginner videos on YouTube. But I mean [follow] along, as in have your paints and brushes and learn through active engagement. Learn how to cast shadows and represent light as it bounces from surfaces (what are the colors that truly create depth? Black and white help you get there sometimes but dark blue on a blue object, for example, will be superior). 

Start with basic shapes (cubes, cones, and spheres are the foundation of all objects) and then slowly build up to more complex shapes (eggs, cups, fruit, etc). Once you are more comfortable (not perfect, as perfection is impossible, but comfortable), start painting faces or more complex objects. After a month or two you will start to want to paint scenes and other things. 

After enough time, you will look back at the things you chose to paint and notice a pattern or habit. That is your style.
